output:
Short answer — choose an LED task lamp with high lumens-per-watt, good color quality (CRI ≥ 90), neutral color temperature (≈3500–4000 K), dimmable controls, and (if useful for your office) occupancy/auto-off or USB charging. Those features give the best energy savings while keeping comfortable, accurate light for office work.

What I checked in your catalog
- I found a product entry named "Meadowlight Lamp" plus generic entries for adjustable desk lamps / task lamps / office lighting. I could not find detailed provenance or spec sheets for Meadowlight Lamp in memory (no source/extractor info). That means I may have an item name in the catalog but no verifiable technical specs. Any specific claims about Meadowlight’s wattage, lumens, CRI, certifications, or controls need verification from the product spec sheet or vendor.

Recommended target specs (use these when comparing models)
- Light source: integrated LED (not incandescent or halogen).
- Power: ~5–15 W for a desk task lamp (depends on desired brightness).
- Brightness: 600–1,200 lumens for typical desk tasks (adjust according to your workspace and screen vs. paper work).
- Efficacy: ≥80 lm/W (higher is better; many modern LEDs are 100+ lm/W).
- Color temperature: 3500–4000 K for neutral white office light (3000 K too warm; 5000 K may appear harsh).
- Color rendering: CRI ≥ 90 for accurate color and comfortable viewing.
- Dimming: smooth, flicker-free dimming (look for specifications about dimmer type and flicker/ PWM).
- Controls: multi-level dim, timer or motion/occupancy sensor if you want extra energy savings.
- Lifetime: rated L70 ≥ 35,000–50,000 hours.
- Certifications: ENERGY STAR or DesignLights Consortium (DLC) listed for verified energy performance.
- Physical: adjustable arm/head, low glare (diffuser or shield), clamp or weighted base to fit the desk.
- Warranty: at least 2–5 years.

Why these matter — evidence summary
- LEDs use far less electrical power than incandescents/halogens for the same light output — typical real-world replacements of a 60 W incandescent with a 10 W LED save ~50 W continuously. Example savings: 50 W × 8 hours/day × 250 workdays ≈ 100 kWh/year per lamp — at $0.13/kWh that’s ≈$13/year saved. (This is a simple illustrative calculation; results depend on your local electricity rates and hours of use.)
- High lm/W (efficacy) directly increases energy efficiency — more useful light per watt.
- CRI and color temperature affect visual comfort and accuracy during tasks; CRI ≥90 is recommended for office tasks that need good color fidelity.
- ENERGY STAR / DLC certifications are independent verifications of stated energy performance; lack of those claims should prompt extra scrutiny.

Claims you should verify for any candidate lamp
- Actual wattage and measured lumens (not just “equivalent to X watt incandescent”).
- Lumens-per-watt (efficacy) and lumen maintenance (L70 hours).
- Measured CRI and correlated color temperature (CCT).
- Dimming performance (is dimming flicker-free? what dimmer types supported).
- Presence and behavior of sensors (occupancy, daylighting) and power draw in standby.
- Third-party certifications: ENERGY STAR, DLC listing, UL/ETL safety ratings.
- Warranty length and service/support terms.

Next steps I can do for you
- If you want, I can look up and compare 3–5 specific models (including Meadowlight Lamp if you want it checked) and list their verified specs and certifications.
- Tell me your preferences: budget per lamp, mounting (clamp vs base), desired brightness range, number of lamps to replace, and whether USB charging or occupancy sensors are important. I’ll pull specific product specs and point out which claims need verification.
